# The first world system: Rome was the customer, Asia the workshop {#sec-ch02}

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
**Preliminary draft --- under review.** Published for review; content, figures and citations may still change.
:::

> *India, the Seres and the Arabian peninsula take from our empire, at the lowest reckoning, a
> hundred million sesterces every year — so dearly do we pay for our luxury and our women.*
> — Pliny the Elder, *Natural History* 12.84 (mid-first century CE)

> *The beautiful ships of the Yavanas came with gold and left with pepper, churning to white foam
> the waters of the Periyar, the river of Kerala.*
> — *Akananuru* 149, Tamil Sangam poetry (1st–2nd century CE)

## Follow one thing: a stream of Roman silver running east {.unnumbered}

The complaint above is the elder Pliny's, written around the middle of the first century CE:
the Roman empire was haemorrhaging precious metal to pay for the luxuries of the East. The
number was rhetorical and much argued over, but the direction was not. Across the early
centuries CE, Roman silver and gold flowed steadily eastward across the Indian Ocean and,
having arrived, largely stayed: it was melted, re-struck by the Kushan and Saka rulers of
north-west India, and absorbed into Asian economies that valued it as metal. Follow that one
stream of metal and you have the argument of this chapter. The richest, hungriest consumer of
the ancient world paid, in hard coin, an economy whose workshops sat not on the Tiber but on
the Tamil coast and beyond. Rome was the customer. Asia was the workshop.^[**Sources:** Pliny, *Natural History* 6.101, 12.84, via Dalrymple, *The Golden Road* (2024); McLaughlin, *The Roman Empire and the Indian Ocean* (2014). **Read more:** De Romanis, *The Indo-Roman Pepper Trade and the Muziris Papyrus* (2020) on what the figures can and cannot bear.]

![Following one thing: Roman silver and gold flowed east toward the workshop, and goods flowed west. Author's schematic.](book/figures/bullion-drain.png){#fig-bullion width=88%}

## Where we are on the arc {.unnumbered}

In @sec-ch01 there was no centre to find — only loosely linked riverine cores and the slow
diffusion of metals and crops along three nascent channels. This chapter is where, for the
first time, the question of where the centre of gravity lay can actually be asked, because for
the first time the channels fused into a single, measurable trans-Eurasian relay running from
Roman Britain to Han China. The conventional answer was "Rome." This chapter tests that answer
by following the goods and the money, and finds that the connected economy's productive core
lay in Asia, with Rome as its structurally dependent western terminus.^[**Sources:** Findlay & O'Rourke, *Power and Plenty* (2007), ch. 1. **Read more:** Beaujard, *The Worlds of the Indian Ocean*, vol. 1 (2019).]

![Centre-of-gravity locator (c.150 CE): Asia the production core of a multipolar relay; Rome the western consumer-terminus. Author's schematic.](book/figures/cog-locator-02.png){#fig-cog02}

![The Eastern Hemisphere about 1 CE — Rome, Parthia, the Kushans and Han China. Map: T. Lessman, worldhistorymaps.net, CC BY-SA 3.0.](book/figures/photos/map_empires_1ce.jpg){#fig-empiresmap width=92%}

## The stage and the cast

The right mental picture is not a wheel with Rome at the hub and spokes running out to
the provinces and beyond. It is a triangle — Rome, India and China — connected by a relay
of intermediary empires, each of which took its cut. The main chain ran Rome to Parthia and the
Kushans to Han China; Aksum (in the Red Sea), the Arabian incense kingdoms, the Indian
states and the island of Sri Lanka, where the ocean's two halves met, rounded out the cast. No single merchant or polity ran the system end to end. It was a
relay of empires, not one market — a distinction we will need when we ask, later, whether
this was really "one" world economy.^[**Sources:** Findlay & O'Rourke (2007), ch. 1; McLaughlin (2014). **Read more:** Abu-Lughod, *Before European Hegemony* (1989), on the "relay" structure of pre-modern world systems.]

The cast of this chapter — India, Sri Lanka, Han China, Parthia and the Kushans, Rome, and the
smaller players around the rim — is profiled below. Following the module's vantage, the profiles run
from east to west: the direction in which the system's goods were made and toward which its
bullion flowed. Click any actor to expand how its economy worked, at home and in the relay;
India, present in every chapter of this book, is given the fullest treatment.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## India — the production core

India in this period was not a single polity but a layered economy spread across the
subcontinent. In the north, the Mauryan empire (c.320–185 BCE) governed a territory administered from
Pataliputra through provincial headquarters at Taxila, Ujjain, Tosali and Suvarnagiri, each under a
prince — which is what Ashoka's own inscriptions attest. The fuller picture of a centralised
fiscal state comes from the *Arthasastra*, and cannot be used here: Olivelle dates that text to the
first or second century CE, four centuries after Chandragupta, and says in terms that its date forbids
using it to reconstruct the Mauryan period. Nor was the extraction the first — Kaul credits the
Nandas before them, while noting that the details are lost — the largest city in South Asia
by some distance, though how large is a question worth pausing on (see below) — and tied together by royal roads running from
Taxila in the north-west to the Bay of Bengal port of Tamralipti. After the Mauryas fragmented,
economic weight shifted south and west: the Satavahanas held the Deccan, while the Tamil
kingdoms of the far south — Chera, Chola and Pandya — commanded the Malabar pepper coast that
Rome most wanted. To the north-west, the Kushans straddled the Hindu Kush and the overland road
to China.^[**Sources:** Roy (p.24) on the Mauryan state; Kaul, "Regional study: Pataliputra", in *The Cambridge World History*, vol. 4 (2015), pp. 514–36, and Allchin, *The Archaeology of Early Historic South Asia* (1995), pp. 109, 202, on the city's size and how it is estimated; Dalrymple (Loc 799) on Ashoka's roads; Roy (p.32) and Dalrymple (Loc 1550) on the southern kingdoms and the Kushan passes. **Read more:** Kaul (2015), for a South Asianist's account of the city.]

How large Pataliputra was is not a question the evidence answers, and following the number back is
the most useful thing this chapter can do with it. The figure in general circulation rests on a lost
book, reported by two later writers, translated in 1877, converted into an area, and multiplied by a
density coefficient borrowed from Mesopotamia. Which line on the ground counts as the city --- the
moat, or the outer ramparts --- moves the answer from about 41,000 people to about 264,000 --- and the area
Megasthenes actually describes, on the same coefficient, gives about 540,000. That is a spread of
some thirteen to one, with no new evidence involved and the same authorities cited at more than one
point on it. Kaul,
writing the *Cambridge World History* entry, takes the moat and concludes that well over 40,000
people lived there in the Mauryan period, and calls even that conservative. What survives the
problem is the hierarchy rather than the number: the same conventions put Rajagriha, Toshali,
Ujjayini and Taxila below it --- though those are grade bands rather than measurements, so the
order within them is firmer than the gaps between them. Even the comparison across
periods is boundary-dependent, and worth doing carefully: measured moat to mound, Pataliputra
was under twice the size of Mohenjo-daro; measured rampart to mound, roughly tenfold. The
secure statement is that the Early Historic cities were the larger, not by how much. The derivation is set out step by step in @sec-appD.^[**Sources:** Kaul,
"Regional study: Pataliputra", in *The Cambridge World History*, vol. 4 (2015), pp. 514--36; Allchin,
*The Archaeology of Early Historic South Asia* (1995), pp. 109, 202; Adams, *Heartland of Cities*
(1981), for the density coefficient. **Read more:** @sec-appD, for the chain in full.]

As everywhere in this period, the base of the economy was agriculture and the village. What set
India apart was the unusually developed commercial and craft sector built on top of it — and, in
particular, the two export industries that would define the subcontinent for the next eighteen
centuries: cotton textiles and pepper. The Malabar coast was the world's principal source of
pepper for roughly fifteen centuries, a spice so woven into Roman cooking that around four-fifths
of the 478 recipes in the cookbook of Apicius called for it; the Latin and Greek words for pepper
and ginger were themselves Tamil loans. Production and long-distance exchange were organised
through merchant guilds (the *śreṇi*) and, distinctively, through Buddhist monasteries placed on
the trade routes, which took perpetual endowments (*akshaya-nivi*) and lent at interest —
proto-financial institutions endowed by the merchant class, and known from the donative
inscriptions at Nasik and Karle.^[**Sources:** Eaton (Loc 3659) on Malabar pepper; Dalrymple (Loc 1294, 1298) on Apicius and the Tamil loan-words; on guilds and monastic finance, Schopen (1997, 2004), Ray (1994) and Neelis (2011), with the Nasik (Ushavadata) and Karle (Bhutapala; Yavana donors) inscriptions. **Read more:** Neelis, *Early Buddhist Transmission and Trade Networks* (2011).]

Behind that commercial sector sat a financial one, and it has a documented institutional form that
is worth setting out, because the usual account of ancient South Asian trade stops at goods and
ports. Craft production was organised in guilds — the *śreṇi* — and the donative inscriptions of the
western Deccan caves name them by trade: weavers, potters, oil millers, and dealers in water-lifting
machines at Govardhana. Guilds gave as institutions, in their own names.

The instrument that mattered most was the perpetual endowment, the *akṣaya-nīvī*. A donor gave a
monastery a capital sum which was never to be spent; the monastery lent it out at interest, and the
interest paid in perpetuity for whatever the donor had specified — lamps, robes, food for the monks,
repairs to the buildings. At Kanheri most donations take this form, in sums running from a couple of
hundred kahapanas upward; one inscription records the purchase of a field for four thousand
kahapanas to fund food for the cave's residents, another a payment of twelve kahapanas each for the
monks' clothing.

What makes this economics rather than piety is that the lending was regulated in writing, and the
regulation survives. The monastic code sets out how such a loan is to be made, and puts the
instruction in the Buddha's own mouth: a pledge of twice the value of the loan is to be taken, a
contract written that carries a seal and is witnessed, and the contract is to record the year, the
month, the day, the name of the Elder of the Community, the Provost of the monastery, the borrower,
the property pledged and the interest. The pledge itself is to be lodged with a trustworthy layman.
That is two-hundred-per-cent collateralisation, a dated and witnessed written instrument naming both
parties and the security, a stated interest rate, and a third party holding the collateral — a
secured loan with an escrow agent, in a religious rulebook, in the first centuries CE.

Gregory Schopen's point about why it existed is the one to carry forward. An endowment lent at
interest is a solution to the problem of keeping an institution alive after the people who funded it
are dead. Monasteries in this period were not incidental to the commercial economy of the western
Deccan; they were where its capital was parked, and they had the legal machinery to lend it.^[**Sources:**
Ray, *Monastery and Guild: Commerce under the Sātavāhanas* (1986), for the named guilds at Govardhana,
the predominance of *akhayanivi* perpetual endowments among the Kanheri donations, the four-thousand-
kahapana field bought by Usavadata and the twelve-kahapana clothing payments; Schopen, *Buddhist
Monks and Business Matters* (2004), for the Vinaya passage on accepting permanent endowments and
lending them at interest, and for the loan-contract instructions attributed to the Buddha. Ray's
reported upper bound for the Kanheri endowments differs between two passages of her own text, so no
maximum is given here. **Read more:** Schopen (2004).]

India's monetary arrangements told the centre-of-gravity story in miniature. Indian states
minted their own coin — punch-marked silver in the north, local issues in the south — but they
treated incoming Roman gold and silver less as foreign currency to be spent than as bullion to be
valued by weight and, increasingly, melted and re-struck. The incentive was structural: gold
stood at roughly 10 to 1 against silver in India and on the Kushan and Saka frontier, against
about 12 to 1 in Rome, so a given weight of silver carried east bought something like a fifth
more goods. That arbitrage pulled Roman metal in and kept it. The clearest measure of how deep it
ran was that the Kushan ruler Vima Kadphises struck India's first gold coinage on the weight
standard of the Roman aureus — the empire's own bullion, re-minted as the subcontinent's coin.^[**Sources:** McLaughlin, *Indian Ocean* (Loc 4323), on the 10:1-versus-12:1 ratio and the resulting margin; Dalrymple (Loc 1634, 1636) on Vima Kadphises's gold coinage.]

Externally, India was the fulcrum of the whole system — the point where its maritime and overland
arms met. Its trade with Rome ran through three coasts: Barygaza in Gujarat to the north-west,
Muziris and Nelkynda on the Malabar pepper coast, and the Coromandel ports facing the Bay of
Bengal. The same merchants and the same monsoon knowledge also worked the leg eastward to
Southeast Asia and Han China — the third side of the Rome–India–China triangle, and the part of
the system least visible through Roman eyes. The balance of this trade ran heavily in India's
favour, because Rome wanted Indian pepper, cotton, gems and ivory while India wanted little that
Rome made, so the exchange settled in precious metal. So lopsided was it that, on Pliny's
telling, Indian goods resold in Rome for up to a hundred times their price at source, and the
Pandya and Chera kings of the south judged the relationship worth cultivating with embassies to
Rome. India was, in short, where the system's most valued goods were made and where its bullion
came to rest: the production core of the first world system.^[**Sources:** Roy (p.32) on the three coasts; Dalrymple (Loc 1323, 1326, 1335, 1338) on the hundredfold markup and the southern embassies. **Read more:** Dalrymple, *The Golden Road* (2024).]

**Trade profile**

- **Main exports** — pepper and other spices, cotton and fine textiles, gems and semi-precious stones, ivory, pearls.
- **Main imports** — gold and silver coin above all, with smaller volumes of wine, coral, glass and base metals.
- **Export markets** — the Roman Mediterranean to the west (via the Red Sea and Egypt); Han China and Southeast Asia to the east; Arabia and the Gulf.
- **Import sources** — Rome and the wider Mediterranean (bullion, wine, coral, glass); the Gulf and Arabia.^[**Sources:** Casson (ed.), *The Periplus Maris Erythraei* (1989), for the cargo lists; McLaughlin (2014); Dalrymple (2024).]
:::

![India in the first world system: regions, emporia and the two trade arms (stylised; not to scale). Author's schematic.](book/figures/actor-india-t2.png){#fig-india-t2 width=66%}

![Gold coins of the Kushan ruler Vima Kadphises (c. 100–127 CE), struck on the Roman aureus standard — the empire's own bullion re-minted as Indian coin. Wikimedia (Ancient Art), CC BY 2.0.](book/figures/photos/coin_kushan.jpg){width=55%}

## Sri Lanka — the island pivot

The island the Greeks called Taprobane sat where the two halves of the Indian Ocean met, and its
economy was built on that position and on water. Its own record is unusually good. At Anuradhapura,
in the northern dry zone, excavation on the citadel mound has produced one of the best-stratified
urban sequences anywhere in South Asia, and it shows a settlement that grew from something over 18
hectares in the Iron Age of roughly 600 to 450 BCE, to about 26 hectares by 350 BCE, to more than 66
hectares by 275 BCE, reaching a maximum of around 71 hectares in the centuries that this chapter
covers. Ramparts enclosed a cardinally oriented rectangle of about 100 hectares, raised in four
stages to a final bank 4.75 metres high and over 15 metres wide.^[**Sources:** Allchin, *The Archaeology
of Early Historic South Asia* (1995), ch. 9, reporting the Sri Lankan and British excavations at
Anuradhapura Salgaha Watta 2 and Deraniyagala's chronology. **Read more:** Allchin (1995), ch. 9.]

Two findings from that sequence bear on the argument of this book. The first is that the city was
walled and functioning before any plausible Mauryan contact: the earliest rampart dates no later
than the period running from the mid-fourth to the late third century BCE, and the excavator's own
dating is earlier still. The second concerns writing. Inscribed potsherds in early Brahmi, in a
Prakrit language, come from levels that Coningham's team dates to the beginning of the fourth
century BCE — on their account the earliest such evidence anywhere in South Asia.

That matters because of what it displaces. The long-accepted view, running from Bühler in the 1890s
through to the 1990s, was that Brahmi was developed in northern India under Ashoka in the third
century BCE and spread southwards to reach Sri Lanka. If the Anuradhapura dating holds, the script
was in use on the island roughly a century and a half before the Ashokan edicts, and the direction
of travel implied by the older model cannot be right. Coningham's team explicitly reopen the
question of how the script developed and spread, and propose trade rather than imperial diffusion as
the mechanism.

Two cautions belong with this. It rests on radiocarbon from one excavation, and the excavators
themselves record that the project's own advisers were initially sceptical that the inscriptions
could be as old as the dates implied. And a claim that overturns a century of epigraphic orthodoxy
should be taught as a strong, well-published challenge rather than as a settled result. But it is no
longer the thinly-sourced assertion this book carried a few drafts ago, and the wider conclusion
around it is firmer still: the second emergence of cities in South Asia was not simply a product of
Mauryan conquest, nor a purely northern affair.^[**Sources:** Coningham (ed.), *Anuradhapura: The
British-Sri Lankan Excavations at Anuradhapura Salgaha Watta 2*, vol. 1, *The Site* (1999), for the
rampart sequence, the fourth-century BCE Brahmi dating, the displacement of the Bühler-to-von Hinüber
orthodoxy, and the reference to the fuller argument in Coningham et al. (1996) and in vol. 2;
Allchin, *The Archaeology of Early Historic South Asia* (1995), ch. 9, for the occupied-area sequence
and the conclusion about the second urbanisation. **Read more:** Coningham (1999).]

The island's water economy worked at two levels, and it is a useful check on any temptation to
explain South Asian states by irrigation alone. Anuradhapura had three large tanks by the beginning
of the Christian era; a survey of the surrounding province counted just under three thousand village
tanks, averaging two or three acres apiece. The monumental works were a royal duty, the small ones a
local affair that royal patronage reached only later. Beyond the obvious point that no large
settlement could exist in the dry zone without stored water, the evidence does not show irrigation
driving the formation of cities or states here, and it does not support reading Sri Lanka as a
hydraulic society.^[**Sources:** Allchin (1995), ch. 9, on the three large tanks, the village-tank
survey of North Central Province after Brohier (1934), and the argument against a hydraulic reading,
following Thapar. **Read more:** Allchin (1995), ch. 9.]

The hinterland has now been surveyed as well as the city, and it changes the picture of how the
island was administered. Coningham's team describe the monasteries scattered through Anuradhapura's
countryside as "Buddhist Temporalities" — institutions performing a dual role, religious and
secular, acting as administrators of the landscape around them rather than as retreats from it. They
also conclude that the hinterland was organised heterarchically, with resources and authority
contested rather than flowing down a single chain from the capital. Set that beside the monastic
lending described in the India profile above and a pattern emerges across the whole region: in the
early centuries CE the Buddhist monastery was among the most economically consequential
institutions in South Asia, holding capital, administering land, and standing between the state and
the village.^[**Sources:** Coningham (ed.), *Anuradhapura*, vol. 3, *The Hinterland* (2013), for the
"Buddhist Temporalities" formulation and the heterarchical reading of the hinterland landscape.
**Read more:** Coningham (2013).]

Trade sat at a different place from government. The capital was inland and agrarian; the entrepot
was Mantai, historic Mahatittha, a mound of some 30 hectares on the north-west coast, roughly a
hundred kilometres away. Mantai occupied the break-of-bulk point between the western and eastern
halves of the ocean and between the two coasts of India, and that position, rather than any local
produce, is what brought it into being. The separation is worth noting because it is the same
structure the chapter has already met at Barygaza and Muziris, where the ports that handled the
trade were not the seats that governed it.^[**Sources:** Allchin (1995), ch. 9, on Mantai's extent
and its position at the break-of-bulk point; Kantarodai in the Jaffna peninsula, at about 25
hectares, was the third of the island's major centres. **Read more:** Allchin (1995), ch. 9.]

What Rome knew of all this was thin, and the contrast is instructive. The *Periplus* recorded an
island called Palaisimundu, anciently Taprobane, whose northern parts were civilised and which
produced pearls, transparent gems, cotton garments and tortoise shell. It also had the island lying
east to west and stretching nearly to Africa. Casson's verdict on the passage is that its author
plainly had no first-hand knowledge, and Sri Lanka's size was exaggerated by Greek, Roman, Indian
and Arab writers alike. Direct contact was accidental when it came: freedmen of Annius Plocamus were
blown off course near Arabia in Claudius's reign and fetched up on the island, which led to a
Sinhalese embassy reaching Rome. Set the two records side by side and the asymmetry is the point.
The archaeology yields a nine-hundred-year stratified urban sequence; the Roman sources yield an
island of the wrong shape in the wrong place.^[**Sources:** Casson, *The Periplus Maris Erythraei*
(1989), section 61 and the general commentary on Taprobane; Cobb, *Rome and the Indian Ocean Trade*
(2018), on the Plocamus episode and against reading it as the discovery of the monsoon.
**Read more:** Casson (1989).]

**Trade profile**

- **Main exports** - pearls, gemstones, tortoise shell and cotton cloth, with the island also
  passing on goods moving between the Arabian Sea and the Bay of Bengal.
- **Main imports** - Mediterranean and Indian manufactures and coin, reaching the coast through
  Mantai; Roman and imitation coins are known from the island's ports.
- **Export markets** - India on both coasts, the Red Sea and Roman Egypt beyond it, and the Bay of
  Bengal to the east.
- **Import sources** - the same routes reversed, with the western trade largely handled through
  Indian and Arabian intermediaries rather than directly.^[**Sources:** Casson (1989), section 61,
  for the commodity list; Allchin (1995), ch. 9, on Mantai and the coin finds at Kantarodai and
  Mantai. **Read more:** Casson (1989).]
:::

Author's schematic.](book/figures/actor-srilanka-t2.png){#fig-actorsrilanka width=85%}
